queue.claim: On CL-Bench, naive in-context history had the highest normalised gain (25.4 % Sonnet 4.6). With GPT-5.4 held fixed it gained 20.1 %, vs 8.6 % for an ACE playbook (at 3.4x the cost) and 7.8 % for agent-kept notes; Mem0 matched it (20.2 %). Model-authored skills scored 8.1 to 11.5 pp below no skills on SkillsBench.
queue.proposed_experiment: Refines H3 (and borrows H1's harness). H3's three arms are all derived (session summary, Workflow node text, curated briefing from top-3 raw episodes); none is raw history. Add arm 4, raw prior-session history in context up to the executor's window, and arm 0, stateless. Run on CL-Bench Codebase Adaptation (tablib 9 issues, tenacity 10 issues; reward 1 - (steps-1)/max_steps) plus the DreamBench-SWE sequences H1 already uses. Report the CL-Bench gain (stateful minus own-stateless). Predeclare: a derived arm ships as a read surface only if it beats arm 4 by a margin at equal or lower tokens. Where history exceeds the window, arm 4 becomes truncated most-recent history.
queue.why_it_matters: If raw history in the window beats curated briefings, Engram's value is retrieval once history no longer fits, not curation. That changes what Consumer 4 is for. CL-Bench's SE sequences are small and executable, so the added arm is cheap.
queue.decision_it_could_change: whether derived read surfaces (summaries, Workflow text, curated briefings) must beat raw history in context before they ship

decision_chain.reason: Can move B16 (lead) and tests B7 against its strongest simple baseline: CL-Bench found raw in-context history gained more than ACE playbooks and agent notes (20.1 vs 8.6 and 7.8% with GPT-5.4), yet none of H3's arms is raw history, so E-20260927-03 adds raw-history and stateless arms on DreamBench-SWE. Now because H3 and E-20260926-04-r2 are about to decide whether Consumer 4 outputs are read surfaces, and that decision is unsound without this baseline.

experiment.claim:
On multi-session software tasks where prior-session history fits the executor's context window, raw prior-session history in context is at least as good as every derived read surface H3 considers (session summary, Workflow node text, curated briefing from the top-3 raw episodes): no derived arm beats raw history on oracle pass rate with a sequence-clustered 95% interval excluding zero.

arms (same frozen executor, same tools, same task prompts; only the memory block differs):
- Arm 0 (stateless): no prior-session material.
- Arm 1 (session summary): Consumer 4 session summaries of the prior sessions.
- Arm 2 (Workflow text): Consumer 4 Workflow node text extracted from the prior sessions; if Consumer 4 produces no Workflow node for a sequence the block is empty and that is recorded.
- Arm 3 (curated briefing): H3's task-conditioned briefing synthesised from the top-3 raw episodes, with the same curator pin H3 uses.
- Arm 4 (raw history): verbatim prior-session transcripts (task, agent turns, tool results, final diff) in chronological order, up to the executor's window minus a fixed reserve for the current task; if they exceed it, truncated to the most recent material and flagged.
- Sessions 1 of each sequence have no prior history and are run once, shared by all arms; sessions 2 and 3 are run per arm.
experiment.metric: primary: oracle pass rate on sessions 2 and 3 (120 session instances), per arm. Reported for each arm: gain over arm 0 (the CL-Bench stateful-minus-own-stateless measure, normalised as (pass_arm - pass_0) / (1 - pass_0)); input tokens per session (median and p95); executor steps. Secondary: the truncated-history subgroup; CL-Bench Codebase Adaptation normalised gain with reward 1 - (steps - 1)/max_steps when solved, if the dataset is available (directional only, 19 issues in 2 repositories).
experiment.predeclared_margin: for each derived arm d in {1, 2, 3}: `derived_superior(d)` if ci95_low(pass_d - pass_4) > 0; `derived_noninferior_cheaper(d)` if ci95_low(pass_d - pass_4) >= -0.10 and median_tokens_d <= 0.5 x median_tokens_4; `raw_superior(d)` if ci95_high(pass_d - pass_4) < 0. Verdict: derived_wins if any derived_superior; raw_wins if no derived_superior and raw_superior holds for every derived arm; otherwise inconclusive, with each derived_noninferior_cheaper arm listed. The card's rule (a derived arm ships only if it beats raw history at equal or lower tokens) is kept as the ship rule; the non-inferior-and-cheaper finding is reported so the token trade-off is visible, and does not by itself ship a surface.
experiment.kill_criterion: the claim is killed (derived_wins) if any derived arm's pass rate exceeds raw history's with ci95_low > 0. Stop before running (not a result) if H1's DreamBench-SWE harness or H3's arm builders are not frozen, more than 20% of arm 4 sessions need truncation (then the run is not in the fitting regime the claim is about), any pin is missing, or the executor or curator model is also the oracle.

sections.question:
**Does processed memory beat raw history when both fit?**

When past sessions fit in the agent's context, does processing them into summaries or briefings beat just pasting them in?
sections.why_now:
**We are deciding which processed memory forms ship.**

If raw history wins wherever it fits, Engram's value is finding the right history once it no longer fits, not rewriting it. That would change what the condensing job is for. If we do not run this, processed forms can ship without ever facing the simplest baseline.
sections.evidence:
**Weak: short benchmarks, one counterexample, software work not broken out.**

- Continual-learning benchmark (Berkeley, Snorkel): raw history in context captured the most of the available improvement over a no-memory run, at 25.4% (Sonnet 4.6). With GPT-5.4 fixed, raw history got 20.1%, a rewritten playbook 8.6% at 3.4 times the cost ($62.8 vs $18.4), and agent-kept notes 7.8%. But Mem0's extracted memories matched raw history at 20.2%, so "raw beats processed" is not universal. Sequences were short enough to fit in context, and software tasks were not reported separately.
- Skills benchmark: procedures the model wrote for itself before a task lowered pass rates by 8.1 to 11.5 percentage points against no procedures (3 configurations). It did not test procedures learned from past runs.

Beliefs this moves: raw past runs often beat distilled skills, and learned procedures are only a hypothesis. It also checks the belief that curating memory for the task at read time beats condensing it at write time.
sections.reviewer:
**Not blocking: no review has been run yet.**

The spec requires a review before execution, and none exists. Points a review should check (our reading, not a reviewer's):

- The inconclusive outcome carries a product rule. It says no processed form ships where history fits until it is shown no worse than raw history at lower tokens. Power to show "no worse within 10 points" is only 64 to 79%, so inconclusive is a likely result. Approving the spec would in effect set that ship gate.
- "Raw wins" requires raw history to beat all three processed forms, a high bar.
- The card priced this as small; the spec revised it to medium (1,980 agent runs).

Clears when: a first review returns no blocking findings, the inconclusive outcome no longer sets a ship rule, and both prerequisites have freeze dates.
sections.commitment:
**Largest model spend of three, blocked on two unbuilt harnesses.**

- Authorises today: the spec enters the queue under owner T4 and adopts its ship rule on an inconclusive result. Nothing runs until you set the standing policy, a runner exists and a review passes.
- People-days: 4 (3 to add the raw-history and no-memory arms, 1 for analysis). This excludes building the benchmark harness and briefing builders, which belong to planned work.
- Model spend: about $265 for about 88M tokens, capped at 100M tokens (about $300). This uses the same assumed $3 per million tokens as the other briefs.
- Verdict: 2026-11-22, and only if both prerequisites are frozen in time.
- Does not exist yet: the frozen benchmark harness, the frozen briefing builders, the added arms, a budget. Not covered by any budget today.
- Our proposed criteria (not published results): the metric is the share of sessions 2 and 3 whose hidden tests pass (120 sessions, 3 runs each). A processed form wins if its 95% interval is above raw history's. Raw wins only if it is above every processed form.
- Pass: where history fits, no processed form ships ahead of raw history. The condensing job becomes cache or index for longer histories.
- Fail: the winning processed form keeps its place, and the belief is narrowed for engineering work.
- Inconclusive: as written, processed forms are held back where history fits. We recommend that this be your call, not the spec's.
sections.action:
**Defer: the spec presets a ship rule you should decide.**

T4 revises the inconclusive outcome to leave shipping to the desk, obtains a first review, and gives freeze dates for the benchmark harness and briefing builders. It returns to the desk by 2026-10-11. Nothing is lost, because the prerequisites are not built yet.
sections.fits:
**What memory the agent is handed at the start of a task.**

Engram can give an agent its prior sessions in three processed forms. The background job that condenses finished work writes session summaries and step-by-step workflow notes. The curator writes a task-specific briefing. The planned briefing-curation test compares only these processed forms. This experiment adds the obvious baseline: paste the raw prior sessions in, plus a no-memory arm. It reuses the planned multi-session benchmark harness.

lineage.label: Continual Learning Bench: Evaluating Frontier AI Systems in Real-World Stateful Environments (CL-Bench)

queue.claim: Retaining the served evidence does not let a reviewer re-derive the decision by re-running the model. At T=0 on identical cases, frontier models reached the same final decision in only 64 to 94 % of replays on the two valid DFAH benchmarks, and tool-signature identity was 20 to 70 %. On stock serving engines two bit-identical batches disagreed on 9 to 23 % of estimates; batch-invariant kernels removed this (0.0 %, n = 106).
queue.proposed_experiment: Refines P0 (step 3, replay) and H3's "served briefing replayed byte-identical" kill criterion. P0 checks that the served artifact comes back unchanged. It does not check whether the decision made from that artifact can be re-derived. Add one fixture with three arms on the same 50 Spec-to-PR-review decisions, each with its pinned served briefing: (A) re-run on the hosted API at T=0, 3 replays; (B) re-run on a self-hosted open model with batch-invariant kernels, 3 replays; (C) return the recorded output from the receipt. Metric: decision unanimity per case (DFAH DecDet) and tool-signature unanimity. Predeclare: if A's unanimity is under 95 %, the contract promises only C (artifact plus recorded output), and the receipt schema adds output, model id, provider and sampling parameters as required fields.
queue.why_it_matters: B1 says the retained artifacts are sufficient. That is true for "show what was served" and false for "reproduce the decision" on hosted inference. The replay guarantee Engram sells has to name which one it gives, and the receipt schema follows from that choice. The fixture takes about a day on the P0 harness.
queue.decision_it_could_change: whether the receipt must store the model's output, model id, provider and sampling parameters, and whether P0 promises artifact replay only or decision re-derivation

decision_chain.reason: Can move B1 (working): DFAH found frontier decision unanimity of only 64 to 94% at T=0, so retained artifacts may show what was served without letting a reviewer re-derive the decision, and E-20260927-02 measures that on 50 of our Spec-to-PR-review cases. Now because P0 is ratifying the replay contract and receipt schema in weeks 1 to 2, and the fixture is cheap (S) on the P0 harness.

experiment.claim: On our Spec-to-PR-review decisions, re-running the pinned hosted model at temperature 0 on the retained served briefing does not reproduce the recorded decision reliably: fewer than 95% of cases reach a unanimous final decision across 5 replays, while returning the recorded output from the receipt reproduces 100% of cases byte-identical. Retaining served artifacts is therefore sufficient to show what was served and what was decided, not to re-derive the decision.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (hosted re-run): for each case, re-run the pinned hosted model on the pinned served briefing and the same tool surface at temperature 0, seed set where the provider supports one, 5 replays per case. Tool calls are answered from the recorded tool results in the receipt (not live), so only model nondeterminism is measured.
- Arm B (self-hosted, batch-invariant, secondary): the same 5 replays on a pinned open-weights model served self-hosted with batch-invariant kernels enabled. Run only if such an endpoint is available in the quarter; if not, recorded as not run, and the verdict rests on A and C. Arm B answers a different question (can re-derivation be offered at all on controlled serving) and never substitutes for A.
- Arm C (recorded output): return the recorded output from the receipt; check byte identity of briefing and output against the stored sha256 values and that the receipt carries output, model id and version, provider and sampling parameters.
- Held equal across A and B: case set, served briefing bytes, prompt template sha256, tool results, decision schema. The model that recorded the original decision is the arm A pin (same id, version and provider).
experiment.metric: primary: decision unanimity per case (DFAH DecDet with N = 5: 1 if all 5 replays give the same final decision as each other and as the recorded decision, else 0), averaged over cases, for arm A. Secondary: tool-signature unanimity (identical tool names and arguments across replays); agreement of the replay majority with the recorded decision; arm B unanimity; arm C fidelity (share of cases returned byte-identical with all required receipt fields). Final decision = the PR review verdict enum {approve, request_changes, comment_only} extracted by schema, not by a model.
experiment.predeclared_margin: artifact_only if unanimity_A < 0.95 (3 or more non-unanimous cases of 50). rederive_supported if non-unanimous_A == 0 of 50 (one-sided 95% upper bound on the non-unanimity rate about 5.8%, B21) and fidelity_C == 1.0. Otherwise (1 or 2 non-unanimous cases) inconclusive. Arm C must reach fidelity 1.0 for any verdict; a C failure is a receipt defect reported to P0, not a result on B1.
experiment.kill_criterion: the hypothesis (re-derivation is unreliable) is killed by rederive_supported. Stop before running (not a result) if fewer than 50 cases or 15 Specs exist, any case lacks a recorded output or tool results, any pin is missing, or the P0 harness cannot answer tool calls from the receipt.

sections.question:
**Does re-running the model reproduce the decision it made?**

If we re-run the same model on the exact briefing it saw, does it make the same review decision every time?
sections.why_now:
**We are about to write down what "replay" promises customers.**

The receipt format and the replay promise are being fixed now. If re-running is unreliable, the receipt must store the model's actual output, or "reproduce a decision" is a promise we cannot keep. If we do not run this, the promise stays at "the served briefing comes back unchanged" and the receipt does not have to store the output.

The evidence already points to storing the output. You can require those receipt fields now without waiting for this test. The test only decides whether we can promise more.
sections.evidence:
**Moderate: two independent papers agree on direction, not our setting.**

- Financial-agent study (IBM, 2025-era models): frontier models re-run 3 times at temperature 0 on the same case made the same final decision on only 64 to 94% of cases. They made identical tool calls on only 20 to 70%. This covers 2 benchmarks of 50 synthetic cases each, and the author says the numbers do not rank models.
- Replay-noise study (7B open models): on standard serving software, two identical requests sent seconds apart disagreed on 9 to 23% of outputs. With serving code built to give identical results regardless of batching, disagreement was 0.0% on 106 cases.

Neither study tests engineering review decisions or current models. The belief this moves: keeping the served material with source and version is enough for a reviewer to reproduce a decision. The evidence says that holds for "show what was served", not for "re-derive the decision".
sections.reviewer:
**Not blocking: no review has been run yet.**

The spec requires a review before execution, and none exists. Points a review should check (our reading, not a reviewer's):

- The recorded decisions were made on a hosted model version that may since have been retired, which would make the test impossible, not failed.
- Replays answer tool calls from the recorded results. If a replay asks a different question, the answer is empty, so divergence can compound.

Clears when: a first review returns no blocking findings, and the run's machine check passes (50 cases from at least 15 Specs, each with recorded output and tool results, all pins filled).
sections.commitment:
**Queues a small test with the earliest verdict of three.**

- Authorises today: the spec enters the queue under owner T2. Nothing runs until you set the standing policy, a runner exists and the review passes.
- People-days: 3 (2 to build the replay command and freeze the cases, 1 for analysis). Case capture reuses the existing flow.
- Model spend: about $15 for about 5M hosted tokens, capped at 8M tokens (about $24). This uses the same assumed $3 per million tokens as the other briefs. The optional self-hosted arm runs only if such a server exists this quarter, and its compute is not priced here.
- Verdict: 2026-10-25, slipping day for day with any policy delay.
- Does not exist yet: the replay command, receipts that hold outputs and tool results, the model version pin, a budget. Not covered by any budget today.
- Our proposed criteria (not published results), on 50 decisions re-run 5 times each: zero of 50 disagreeing allows re-derivation, which bounds the true disagreement rate below about 5.8%. Three or more disagreeing means artifact only. One or two is inconclusive. Returning the stored output must reproduce 100% of cases, or it is a receipt defect.
- Pass: for that exact hosted model only, Engram may promise re-derivation. The receipt still stores the output.
- Fail: the promise is "show what was served and what was decided". The receipt adds the output, model version, provider and sampling settings as required fields. The belief is narrowed.
- Inconclusive: the artifact-only promise stays as the cautious default, and the test is kept for the next model version.
sections.action:
**Approve: 3 people-days and $15 settle the replay promise.**

This has the lowest cost and earliest verdict of the three briefs, and it fixes the wording of a customer-facing promise. Independently, consider requiring the output fields in the receipt now.
sections.fits:
**The receipt that records what an agent was shown.**

Engram keeps a receipt for every memory it serves: the briefing, where each piece came from and its version. Our planned replay test checks that the briefing comes back byte for byte. This experiment asks whether a reviewer can also re-run the model on that briefing and get the same decision. It also sets the replay criterion used by the planned briefing-curation test.

queue.claim: On our frozen engineering-agent traces, a decision-model pass/fail judge is no worse than our LLM judge on agreement with blinded human labels, has higher failure recall, and flips fewer verdicts across repeated calls, at lower cost per decision.
queue.proposed_experiment: Arm A = current LLM judge (structured verdict + confidence); Arm B = decision-model judge with one binary rubric proposition per trace and a threshold fixed before the run. Dataset: a frozen set of at least 300 of our harness traces, with a blinded human-labelled audit subset sized from B21 (at least 150 traces including at least 50 failures), plus 100 traces x 20 repeats for repeatability. Metrics: human agreement, failure recall on labelled failures, count of traces with verdict flips, cost and p50 latency per decision. Predeclared margin: B within 5 points of A on human agreement (paired bootstrap lower bound >= -5), B failure recall >= A, and B flips <= A. Kill: if B's failure recall is lower than A's by more than 5 points or the agreement lower bound is below -5, keep the LLM judge.
queue.why_it_matters: R6 requires traceable protocols and uncertainty; a judge that is cheap and repeatable enough to run on every change changes how often we can measure, but only if it does not miss failures. The neosigma study (25 vs 17 of 29 failures caught, 3 vs 19 flipped traces) is one team on customer-service traces; our long engineering traces may behave differently.
queue.decision_it_could_change: which judge gates every change in the P3 harness: a decision-model pass/fail judge with LLM explanation of failures only, or an LLM judge on every trace

decision_chain.reason: The judge scores every Track B verdict. The frozen-judge rule means it can only be changed before the next locked round, so now is the time to test it. The spec also measures calibration, which can move B14 (working) with our own data. The only source is one study by a vendor's customer on customer-service traces, and its human audit was inconclusive. So the spec sizes the human audit from B21 (300 test traces, at least 75 failures), raises the cost to M for about 10 people-days of labelling, and requires an egress review before any trace leaves our infrastructure.

Superseding spec E-20260927-01-r2 answers REV-20260927-07 with a provenance allowlist and logged payload checks that keep evaluator outcomes away from both judges, a predeclared invalid-call and retry policy with all-attempt cost and a 0.98 completion floor, a deterministic threshold tie rule, repeat dispatch reconciled with cost, per-split family and failure-cluster minimums with design-effect power and family-level flip bounds, and every missing packet item turned into a machine-checked not_runnable condition. It can still move B14 with a local calibration measurement and decides which judge gates the P3 harness, so it is worth running once policy and the harness exist.

experiment.claim: On our frozen engineering-agent traces, rendered through a provenance allowlist that removes every evaluator-produced outcome, a decision-model pass/fail judge (one binary rubric proposition per trace, threshold fixed on a dev split by a deterministic rule) is non-inferior to our LLM judge on agreement with blinded human labels (95% lower bound of the difference >= -0.05), has failure recall no lower than the LLM judge's, completes at least 98% of calls validly, and flips verdicts on no more traces across repeated calls, at lower all-attempt cost per decision.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (incumbent): the P3 LLM judge, structured output {verdict, confidence, rationale}, pinned model and prompt.
- Arm B: decision-model judge, one yes/no proposition per trace; pass if P(yes) >= tau, where tau is chosen on the dev split by the rule in "Threshold rule" below and frozen in `threshold.json` before any test trace is judged.
- Shared rubric: the same proposition for both arms ("Did the agent complete the task stated in `task` so that its stated acceptance checks would pass?").
- Shared rendering, provenance allowlist: each trace segment carries a `source` tag written by the P3 harness at capture time. Only these sources are rendered: `task` (task statement as given to the agent), `agent_turn` (agent messages and tool calls), `agent_tool_result` (raw output of tools the agent itself invoked during the episode, including tests and CI runs the agent triggered), `agent_diff` (final diff). Always excluded: `evaluator` (post-episode test or CI runs by the harness, hidden acceptance tests and their results), `oracle`, `reward`, `label`, `harness_summary` (any pass/fail or score line appended by the harness), and any segment with no `source` tag. Order and cap: task statement, final diff, agent-triggered test and CI output, then the most recent agent turns until 16,000 tokens. Both arms see a byte-identical payload; capped traces are flagged and analysed as a subgroup.
- Payload checks: after rendering, every payload is scanned for (1) any excluded `source` tag, (2) the trace's oracle id, reward field names and label strings from `labels.jsonl` and `index.jsonl`, (3) the harness's own summary line patterns listed in `leak_patterns.json`. Each check is logged per trace to `payload_checks.jsonl`. A trace that fails any check is excluded from both arms and counted; if more than 2% of traces fail, the run is not runnable (renderer defect, not a result).
- Separation: neither judge model is the agent model that produced the traces, and neither is used as answerer in any run it judges.
- Human labels: every trace labelled pass/fail by one labeller blind to both judges and to the executable oracle result; a second blind labeller on 100 test traces for inter-rater agreement; disagreements adjudicated by a third person. Labellers are not the rubric or threshold author. Labellers see the full trace including evaluator segments only if the labelling protocol says so, fixed in `labelling_protocol.md` before labelling starts; judges never do.

Invalid-call policy (predeclared, both arms):
- A call is invalid if it times out (60 s), returns a transport error, returns output that fails the schema (A: missing or non-enum verdict; B: missing probability), or returns a probability or confidence outside [0, 1] or NaN.
- Each invalid call is retried at most 2 times (3 attempts in total), with the same payload and pins. Every attempt is logged and every attempt's tokens and cost count toward that arm's cost.
- If all 3 attempts are invalid, the judgment is recorded as `invalid`. No trace is dropped. For agreement, `invalid` counts as disagreement with the human label. For failure recall, `invalid` on a human-labelled failure counts as not caught. For flips, `invalid` is a distinct verdict value.
- Valid-completion rate = share of judgments (not attempts) with a valid final result. An arm with valid-completion rate below 0.98 on the test split cannot pass.

Threshold rule (deterministic): candidate thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive distinct P(yes) values on the dev split, plus 0 and 1. Choose the candidate that maximises balanced accuracy against the adjudicated dev labels; among ties, the one with the highest dev failure recall; among remaining ties, the highest tau. `threshold.json` records the candidate list, the chosen tau, the tie-break path taken, a timestamp and its sha256.

Repeat dispatch: the repeat subset is 60 test traces fixed in `index.jsonl` before the run. The test-stage call is call 1 for those traces; the repeat stage makes 9 further calls per trace per arm (calls 2 to 10). Flips are computed over the 10 verdicts per trace. Cost for repeats counts the 9 further calls (plus retries).
experiment.metric: primary: agreement with adjudicated human labels on the test split; failure recall = share of human-labelled test failures judged fail. Guards: valid-completion rate per arm; repeatability = count of repeat traces whose verdict takes more than one value over the 10 calls. Secondary: expected calibration error of B's P(yes) and A's confidence on the test split (10 equal-width bins; this is what can move B14); agreement with the executable oracle where one exists (supporting evidence, not ground truth, computed outside the judge processes); all-attempt cost per decision and p50/p95 latency; capped-trace subgroup; retry counts per arm.
experiment.predeclared_margin: judge_pass requires ci95_low(agree_B - agree_A) >= -0.05 AND (recall_B - recall_A) >= 0 AND ci95_low(recall_B - recall_A) >= -0.10 AND valid_rate_B >= 0.98 AND flips_B <= flips_A AND cost_per_decision_B < cost_per_decision_A (all-attempt cost).
experiment.kill_criterion: keep_llm_judge if (recall_B - recall_A) < -0.05 OR ci95_high(agree_B - agree_A) < -0.05 OR valid_rate_B < 0.95 (the decision model is clearly worse on the endpoint that matters for gating, or unusable). Stop before running (not a result) if any not_runnable condition in the execution packet holds.

sections.question:
**Can a cheap judge catch failures as well as our current one?**

Does a cheap decision-model judge catch at least as many failed agent runs as our LLM judge, and agree with humans as often?
sections.why_now:
**The rebuilt harness picks its gating judge before the next locked round.**

A judge that is cheaper and gives the same verdict on repeat calls lets us score every change, not a sample. A judge that misses failures would let bad changes through. If we do not run this, the LLM judge stays the only gate, at its current cost and with its verdicts sometimes flipping between identical calls.
sections.evidence:
**Weak: one study, one comparator, a different kind of trace.**

One team (a customer of the decision-model vendor) judged 834 customer-service agent runs with both a decision model and GPT-5 Mini. These are published results, not ours:

- Agreement with a blind human reviewer: 88 vs 85 of 100 runs. The gap is inside the noise (95% interval: minus 10.9 to plus 5.1 points), so this shows no difference either way.
- Failures caught: 25 vs 17 of 29 human-labelled failures. This is the result that matters for gating, but it rests on 29 cases.
- Runs whose verdict flipped over 20 identical calls: 3 vs 19 of 100.
- Cost per 10,000 decisions: $3.23 vs $19.98 (6.2 times cheaper). Median latency 231 ms vs 7.8 s.

The decision threshold and model versions were not published. Our runs are long engineering sessions, not short customer chats, so the result may not transfer.

The belief this can move: vendors claim their decision models give calibrated probabilities, but nobody has shown it, so we fit thresholds locally. The belief that zero errors in n cases bounds the error rate at about 3 in n sets the sample sizes and is not moved.
sections.reviewer:
**Blocking: the review asked for revisions and is not yet re-run.**

The review of the first draft returned "revise" with five problems. The revised spec answers four in writing:

1. The judge could see hidden test results, which would leak the answer. Now only material the agent itself produced is shown, and each payload is scanned for leaks.
2. Failed or malformed judge calls had no rule, so dropping them could flatter a judge. Now every failed call counts as wrong and its cost counts.
3. Threshold ties and repeat-call counting were ambiguous. Now fixed by rule.
4. Too few task families to trust the statistics. Now minimum family and failure counts are required, and power is restated for correlated runs.

The fifth problem stays open by design: the harness, labelled traces, pins and budget do not exist yet and cannot until the work is scheduled. Approval is still the right call because it only queues the spec. A machine check refuses to run while any of these is missing.

Clears when: a re-review confirms fixes 1 to 4, and the run's machine check passes (400 labelled traces, at least 75 test failures across at least 10 task families, all pins filled, a dollar cap set).
sections.commitment:
**Queues the comparison; nothing is labelled, built or spent yet.**

- Authorises today: the spec enters the queue under owner T3. Nothing runs until you set the standing policy, a runner exists and the re-review clears.
- People-days: 16 (10 for human labelling, 2 for tagging trace sources and leak patterns, 3 to build the comparison command (our estimate, not in the spec), 1 for analysis).
- Model spend: about $100 for about 33M tokens, capped at 40M tokens (about $120). All three briefs use one assumed rate of $3 per million tokens because no price list is staged.
- Verdict: 2026-11-27, slipping day for day with any policy delay.
- Does not exist yet: the comparison command, the 400 frozen traces, the labels, the pins, a budget. The labelling time is not covered by any budget today.
- Our proposed pass (not published results): the decision model's human agreement is no more than 5 points below the LLM judge's (95% lower bound). It must also catch at least as many failures, complete at least 98% of calls, flip on no more runs and cost less. Power is about 73%, so a truly equal judge has roughly a one in four chance of reading inconclusive.
- Pass: the decision model gates every run from the next locked round, and the LLM judge explains failures only. Past verdicts are not silently re-scored.
- Kill (catches 5 or more points fewer failures, clearly worse agreement, or under 95% valid calls): the LLM judge stays the gate.
- Inconclusive: the LLM judge stays as the default, not as proof it is better. The decision model may run alongside it to grow the labelled failure set.
sections.action:
**Approve: tight revised spec, and approval only queues it.**

The spec answers every fixable review point, and the machine check blocks execution until the missing data and re-review exist. The 10 labelling days are the real cost, so allocate them when you set the policy.
sections.fits:
**The judge that marks each agent run pass or fail.**

Our evaluation harness is being rebuilt after its labels leaked into scoring. Every change to Engram is scored by an LLM judge that reads a finished agent run and says pass or fail. This experiment tests whether a small, fast decision model could do that job instead, with the LLM judge kept only to explain failures.

queue.claim: On H10's seeded history, the "still true given the snapshot?" audit reaches at least 0.10 higher stale-flag precision at recall >= 0.7 when items are stored as decision records with a date and a reason than when the same items are stored as bare facts, and a "not updated in more than two weeks" age flag scores below both.
queue.proposed_experiment:
Arm A = age flag: mark anything not updated in more than two weeks (rvaniaaaa's daily compilation recipe). Arm B = bare facts: each item stored as a one-line fact with a timestamp, audited with jevmem's noul ("Is memory X still true for this repository, given the snapshot?"; true = consistent or no evidence against, false = the file, dependency or approach it names is gone or replaced), flag below 0.4. Arm C = decision records: the same items stored as decision, date and reason (JeffWitters: "A decision arrives with a date and a reason attached, so when it stops being true there is something to check it against"), audited with the same noul given the reason. Arm D = source-change invalidation (H10a's required first control): flag an item when a file or dependency it cites changes. Dataset: H10's ~50 Decisions whose underlying file or dependency later changes and ~50 that stay valid, each authored once and rendered in both B and C forms; snapshot per jevmem (tree to depth 3, package.json fields, first 3,000 chars of README) plus the diff of cited files. Metrics: stale-flag precision and recall, threshold fit on half and tested on the other half; audit tokens per item. Predeclared margin: C - B >= 0.10 precision at recall >= 0.7, A below B. Kill: C - B below 0.05 (the reason field is not worth making mandatory), or D matches C (source-change invalidation suffices and the model audit is not needed, which H10a already names as a kill).

Evidence: all four practitioner posts behind this rule are opinions with 0 to 1 likes and 7 to 25 views; the questions "Does storing reasons with decisions measurably reduce stale-entry retrieval? Not tested." and how jevmem's file behaves over weeks ("false `[stale?]` flags ... Not measured") are open in the notes. jevmem lines carry a timestamp and confidence but no free-text reason field, and its snapshot is shallow, so memories about code internals get "no evidence against it" and pass.

The result decides whether P5 makes `reason` mandatory and gives H10a a representation arm; it could seed a new register belief, since no current belief covers record representation.

experiment.arms:
- Arm A (age flag): flag any item not updated in more than 14 days (rvaniaaaa's daily compilation recipe).
- Arm B (record without reason): decision text, decided_at, cited files, rendered from a fixed template; audited with jevmem's noul ("Is memory X still true for this repository, given the snapshot?"; true = consistent or no evidence against it; false = the file, dependency or approach it names is gone or replaced).
- Arm C (record with reason): Arm B's exact rendering plus one line "reason: <reason text>" at a fixed position; nothing else changes. Same audit model, prompt, batch composition and order as B.
- Arm B0 (bare fact, secondary, descriptive only): the one-line fact form from r1, kept so the r1 comparison can still be reported; it is not used in any verdict.
- Arm D (source-change invalidation, H10a's required first control): flag an item when a file or dependency it cites changes.
- Snapshot for B, B0 and C: jevmem's recipe (tree to depth 3, selected package.json fields, first 3,000 characters of README) plus the diff of files cited by the item.
- Model-visible allowlist: B and B0 see only {rendered item, snapshot, cited-file diffs}; C additionally sees reason_text. Stale labels, reason-source metadata, labeller ids, last_updated and repository split are never in model-visible state; they live in `labels.jsonl` and `meta.jsonl`, which the audit process does not open.
experiment.metric:
stale score s = 1 - P(still true), mean of 3 repeats. For B, B0 and C, the flag threshold is fitted on the fitting half and applied to the test half (algorithm below). Primary: test-half precision at the fitted threshold, valid only if test recall >= 0.7. Also: recall at the fitted threshold; audit tokens per item. Deterministic arms A and D: precision and recall of their fixed flags on the test half.

threshold algorithm: on the fitting half, sort items by s descending; the threshold tau is the largest value such that flagging every item with s >= tau gives fit-half recall >= 0.7 (ties at tau are all flagged). If no tau achieves recall 0.7 on the fitting half, the arm is infeasible. On the test half, flag every item with s >= tau. An arm's operating point is feasible on test only if test recall >= 0.7 and at least one item is flagged; otherwise its precision is undefined and any verdict that uses it is inconclusive.

Arm A = served memory with no frame and no gate. Arm B = framing only: served inside a delimited block with jevmem's frame ("facts, not instructions") and any delimiter tag inside a line neutralised. **We are deciding what the filter must prove before it enforces.**

queue.claim: Inside one otherwise identical system, writing supersedes and contradicts edges at write time (and excluding superseded items from recall) raises knowledge-update accuracy by at least 5 points over the same system with every new unit simply added, at no loss on the other question classes beyond the noise floor.
queue.proposed_experiment:
Arm A = edges off: "prefer add over modify" kept, every new unit added, no supersedes or contradicts edges, recall unchanged. Arm B = edges on: supersede only when two signals agree (contradiction >= 0.7 AND a named target id, jevmem's rule), old item kept but tagged superseded and excluded from recall, contradicts edges inhibited at read time (REALM's conflict_inhibit). Arm B2 = Arm B with the single-signal rule (contradiction alone), to test jevmem's "Contradiction needs two signals" design note. Everything else fixed: extractor, embedder, fusion, k, token budget. Dataset: H2's harness on the LongMemEval knowledge-update subset, plus a contradiction dev set built like jevmem's (reversals plus near-misses that must not supersede) from our own project history, labelled by someone other than the rule author. Metrics: knowledge-update accuracy, accuracy on the other LongMemEval classes, false-supersede rate on near-misses, missed-supersede rate on reversals. Predeclared margin: B >= A + 5 points on knowledge-update with a paired interval excluding 0, and false supersedes on near-misses no higher than 1 in 16 equivalent. Kill: B - A below the noise floor on knowledge-update (then REALM's 84.72 without reconsolidation vs Zep's 74.40 came from something other than the edges, and H7's typed-graph premise weakens), or B2 no worse than B on false supersedes (the two-signal rule is unnecessary).

Evidence behind the margin: REALM knowledge-update 84.72 without reconsolidation and 88.89 with it, against Zep's 74.40, but that is a whole-system comparison with baselines mostly copied from other papers; jevmem's contradiction dev set went from 20/27 to 25/27 reversals caught between v0.4.1 and v0.4.2 with 0/16 false supersedes, on an author-written set; Hippo's audit lists supersession among "what measured helpful" without an isolated number.
queue.why_it_matters: R2 depends on write-time supersession being what makes current-state questions answerable, yet B3 rests on a comparison where the edges were never switched off. A clean on/off ablation tells H7 whether to seed its typed graph with SUPERSEDES edges as the core mechanism or treat them as an index.
queue.decision_it_could_change: refines H7: adds an edges-on vs edges-off ablation inside one system on the LongMemEval knowledge-update subset, so B3's isolated contribution is measured instead of inferred from a whole-system comparison with Zep

decision_chain.reason: Spec E-20260926-07 turns write-time supersedes and contradicts edges on and off inside one system, on LongMemEval and our own PDLC knowledge-update questions, and tests the two-signal supersede rule. It can move B3 (lead), which rests on a whole-system comparison with Zep. It must land before the supersession MVP and H7 build a typed graph around SUPERSEDES; cost M.

Revision r2 answers REV-20260926-22 and REV-20260926-25. Conclusions are limited to our local intervention, with no claim about REALM vs Zep. A 2 x 2 factorial separates supersession from inhibition over a common logged candidate history. The contradiction test set stays sealed until the rule is frozen. The primary design runs on PDLC histories only (about 27M tokens, hard cap 35M), with a 5-point non-inferiority margin it has the power to test. It can give B3 (lead) its first isolated local measurement before H7 builds on it. It still needs P5's superseded state, a frozen H2 harness, about 8 people-days of labelling and a policy. experiment.claim: Inside our system, with everything else fixed, write-time supersession (superseded items kept but excluded from recall) together with contradicts-edge inhibition at read time raises knowledge-update accuracy on our PDLC histories by at least 5 points over the same system with every new unit simply added, with other question classes non-inferior within 5 points. Conclusions apply to this local intervention only; they do not identify what caused REALM's whole-system gap over Zep.
experiment.arms:
- Edge construction (shared by every arm): each new unit is processed once, in ingestion order, against a common immutable candidate history: the up-to-10 candidates are retrieved from the edges-off store (all prior units, nothing suppressed), so candidate sets never depend on an arm's earlier suppression. One pinned decision call per unit returns contradiction score c in [0, 1], relation in {supersedes, contradicts, none} and target id among the candidates (or null). Calls, candidates and outputs are logged once; every arm is materialised by applying its rule to the same log.
- Rules applied to the log:
  - supersede edge (two-signal): c >= 0.7 AND relation = supersedes AND target id not null.
  - supersede edge (single-signal, B2 only): c >= 0.7, target = top-ranked candidate, relation ignored.
  - contradicts edge: c >= 0.7 AND relation = contradicts AND target id not null.
- 2 x 2 factorial plus a rule variant:
  - A (neither): every unit added; edges not used at read time.
  - S (supersession only): superseded items tagged (P5 `superseded` state) and excluded from recall; contradicts edges ignored.
  - I (inhibition only): contradicts edges dropped from expansion at read time (REALM's conflict_inhibit); superseded items not excluded.
  - B (both): S and I together; the primary bundle.
  - B2: as B but with the single-signal supersede rule.
- Everything else fixed: extractor, embedder, fusion, k, token budget, answerer and judge. No oracle-session warm-up (REALM A.4's path is excluded): every store is built only from the history before the question's cut-off time. Answerer and judge are pinned models from different families from each other and from the decision model; the judge sees only (question, answer, reference), with arm labels stripped.
experiment.metric: primary: knowledge-update accuracy (blinded judge) on PDLC knowledge-update questions. Non-inferiority: accuracy on PDLC other-class questions asked against the same stores. Rule quality on the sealed contradiction test set: false-supersede rate on near-misses and missed-supersede rate on reversals, each with a Clopper-Pearson interval. Secondary: factorial main effects of S and I; LongMemEval_S knowledge-update accuracy (78 questions) if the optional stage runs; served tokens.
experiment.predeclared_margin: bundle_helps requires (ku_B - ku_A) >= 0.05 with the 95% cluster-bootstrap interval excluding 0, AND ci95_low(other_B - other_A) >= -0.05, AND on the sealed test set ub95(false-supersede rate of B) <= 0.05 (at least 90 near-misses; 1 or fewer false supersedes is needed). Component attribution (reported, not a gate): the S and I main effects with intervals; a component is called "carrying" only if its main-effect interval excludes 0. Rule choice on the sealed test set: two_signal_needed if fs_B2 - fs_B >= 3 with one-sided exact McNemar p < 0.05; two_signal_costly if missed_B - missed_B2 >= 3 with one-sided exact McNemar p < 0.05; otherwise rule_choice_inconclusive, with the two-signal rule kept as the operational default (not a finding of equivalence).
experiment.kill_criterion: bundle_bounded: ub95(ku_B - ku_A) < 0.05. Stop before running (not a result) if P5's `superseded` state is not implemented, H2's harness is not frozen, any count minimum is not met, the sealed test set was opened before the rule was frozen, any gold or reference text is in a store, or any pin is missing.

sections.question: When we mark old memories as replaced, do agents answer "what is true now?" questions better?
sections.why_now:
**The typed memory graph is about to be built on this.**

Our belief is that these links help answer update questions, but the only evidence is a whole-system comparison where they were never switched off. If we skip this, the graph is built on that unmeasured premise.

**Write-time marking of which memory replaces which.**

When a new memory contradicts or updates an old one, Engram can mark the old one as replaced and hide it from recall. This test switches that marking on and off inside our own system. It refines the planned typed memory graph, which would be built around these links.

queue.claim: On our corpus, a single listwise decision-model choice call over the fused pool beats a local cross-encoder by at least 3 points of end answer accuracy at 5 served memories, not only on recall@1.
queue.proposed_experiment:
Arm A = one choice call over the whole pool, rank positions used as scores (Hindsight design). Arm B = one yes/no call per candidate, batched into one request, sorted by probability (the pointwise design Hindsight measured against). Arm C = local cross-encoder ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 (Hindsight's default and Hippo's fallback). Arm D = one self-hosted reranker from the SciFact chart (bge-v2-m3 or mxbai-large). Candidate order and pool identical across arms; PC-20260926-03's order control applies to Arm A. Dataset: P3 held-out set plus 100 build-time read queries from P0 fixtures, 30 and 240 candidates per query. Metrics: end answer accuracy by the frozen judge at 2 and at 5 served memories (primary), recall@1, recall@5, cost per query, p50 and p95 latency. Predeclared margin: A >= C + 3 points answer accuracy at 5 memories with a paired, task-clustered interval excluding 0. Kill: A within the noise floor of C or D at 5 memories (then the hosted call's only benefit is a shorter context and its egress risk is not justified), or A below B on recall@1 (B10 does not replicate).

The notes disagree on what the rerank buys. Hindsight: recall@1 0.94 listwise vs 0.87 pointwise at a thirtieth of the calls on 200 LoCoMo questions, and 0.950 vs 0.800 against local MiniLM at 30 candidates (0.583 to 0.783 at 240). Hippo: R@1 0.6167 vs cross-encoder 0.4133 on a private 300-query store, but graded answers at 5 memories were tied (Jev vs CE -0.0067; "An answer win over the free cross-encoder was not shown"), with the gain appearing only at 2 memories (base 0.0867, CE 0.1067, Jev 0.1400). Supermemory: Jev Score-10 at approx. 0.746 nDCG@10 on SciFact against approx. 0.735 to 0.766 for self-hosted rerankers at roughly a tenth of the cost.
queue.why_it_matters: R4 asks that a decision model take over only where it beats the cheap alternative on the outcome we care about, and every positive rerank number in the catalogue is a retrieval metric while the one answer-level test was a tie. The result decides whether the rerank sends memory text to a hosted API at all.

It decides now whether memory text leaves our infrastructure for reranking; cost revised from S to M.

Revision r2 answers REV-20260926-21. The local reranker is chosen on a separate dev split before test. The judge is a separate model and is blinded. The run follows an exact dispatch list (about 32M tokens). B10's LoCoMo result is left intact, and the answer-level and call-shape results are recorded separately. experiment.arms:
- Arm 0 (reference): RRF fusion order, no rerank.
- Arm A: one listwise choice call over the whole pool; rank positions are the scores (Hindsight design, B10's shape).
- Arm B: one yes/no question per candidate, all in a single request, sorted by probability (the hev/reranker "Noul batch" shape). This is NOT the separate-call pointwise design B10 measured against; the call-count comparison in B10 is not tested here. Pool 30 only.
- Arm C: local cross-encoder ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2.
- Arm D: self-hosted bge-reranker-v2-m3.
- Arm L*: whichever of C and D has higher accuracy at 5 memories on the dev split; chosen once, written to `selection.json` and frozen before any test query is scored. The unselected local arm is not run on test.
- Shared: identical pool per query, candidate text truncated to 120 tokens for every arm (keeps the 240 pool under the decision model's 32,000-token context), identical seeded candidate order; order control on a 100-query test subset with two further orders for Arm A; the answerer and the judge are pinned models from different families from each other and from the decision model; the judge sees only (question, answer, reference) with arm labels stripped.

dispatch (exact; nothing else is run):
- dev (150 queries): pool 30; arms C, D; served 5; answerer and judge.
- test pool 30 (700 queries: 600 P3 + 100 P0): arms 0, A, B, L*; served 2 and 5; answerer and judge. Rankings for A and B also scored for nDCG@10 and recall@k.
- test pool 240 (fixed seeded 200-query subset of the 600 P3): arms 0, A, L*; served 5; answerer and judge.
- order control (fixed seeded 100-query subset): Arm A only, pool 30, two extra orders, rankings only.
experiment.metric: primary: end answer accuracy by the blinded judge at 5 served memories on test pool 30, Arm A vs L*. Secondary: accuracy at 2 served memories; pool 240 accuracy; recall@1 and recall@5 against gold evidence; decision-model tokens and cost per query; p50 and p95 latency. Separate result (from PC-20260927-03): nDCG@10 and gold recall@5 for Arm B vs Arm A on test pool 30, split by number of gold-relevant items (exactly 1 vs at least 3).

sections.question: Does paying a hosted model to rank memories give better agent answers than a free local ranker?
sections.why_now:
**This decides whether memory text leaves our infrastructure.**

Every favourable number so far measures retrieval, not answers. If we skip this, the working default is a local reranker: no egress, no per-call cost, and no evidence it is good enough.
sections.evidence:
**Weak: vendor retrieval scores, plus one answer-level tie.**

One vendor reports the hosted pick found the right memory first 94% of the time, against 87% for per-item yes/no questions and 80% for a local reranker. A second system saw a large first-hit gain (0.62 versus 0.41) but tied the local reranker on graded answers at 5 memories. These details were unavailable to the reviewer. A pinned repository found per-item yes/no beats one pick when many items are relevant.

sections.fits:
**The reranker that picks which memories an agent sees.**

After retrieval, a reranker orders candidates and the top 2 or 5 are served. The options: one call to a hosted decision model that picks from the whole list, or a free reranker we run ourselves. It refines the planned reranker, which the plan names but never defines.

lineage.label: We Added Jev as a Reranker. Here's What We Learned

queue.claim: On our held-out set, a ranker with no "none" option that always returns at least one memory, placed behind a separate recall/no-recall gate, keeps gold retention within 0.02 of the ungated ranker on answerable queries and abstains correctly on unanswerable queries at least 20 points more often, whereas a ranker with a "none" option loses at least 0.05 gold retention.
queue.proposed_experiment:
Arm A = choice rerank over the fused pool with no "none" option, at least 1 memory always served (Hindsight's shipped design). Arm B = the same choice with an added "none" option and a minimum probability of 0.05, serving nothing when nothing clears it (jevmem's shipped recall: "No listed memory is relevant to the query."). Arm C = Arm A behind a separate yes/no "does this prompt need memory?" gate evaluated before retrieval (Supermemory's UserPromptSubmit gate, which honours "without using memory, tell me..."). Dataset: P3 held-out set with answerable, unanswerable and explicit opt-out prompts, pools from H2's fusion. Metrics: gold retention and empty-result rate on answerable queries, correct abstention on unanswerable and opt-out prompts, end answer accuracy. Predeclared margins as in the claim. Kill: B's gold retention within 0.02 of A (the Hindsight failure does not reproduce on our pools, so the split in B11 is unnecessary), or C's abstention gain under 10 points (a pre-retrieval gate is not worth its call).

The notes disagree: Hindsight's "none of these" option emptied 35 of 200 questions and a "nothing is relevant" Score level emptied 7% of queries and dropped gold retention from 0.81 to 0.65, and Supermemory's Noul used as a keep/delete gate "kept nothing"; jevmem's design rule is the opposite ("Every choice has a `none` option") and it has no recall-quality measurement ("Recall quality is not measured"). Supermemory's recall gate has no accuracy, latency or cost numbers.
queue.why_it_matters: R4 says a decision is automated only when its error behaviour is understood, and two shipped systems make opposite choices about where "nothing relevant" lives with no measurement on the abstention side. The result fixes the rerank-vs-admission split in B11 and tells P0 F10 whether an empty result should come from a gate or from the ranker.

Revision r2 answers REV-20260926-20. The ranker arms are now a none-option x cutoff factorial, so cutoff losses are not blamed on the none option. Unanswerable abstention and opt-out compliance are separate endpoints, with a deterministic opt-out rule as the control. Answerer, judge and ranker are separate models, the judge is blinded and gold stays out of the store. It can give B11 (working) our own measurement of where the empty result belongs. The vendor numbers stay unverified, the harness does not exist and policy is unset, so this sets priority and does not approve a run.

experiment.claim: On our held-out set, (1) adding a "none" option to a listwise choice ranker, with the probability cutoff and serving policy held fixed, lowers gold retention on answerable queries by at least 0.05; (2) a separate pre-retrieval recall/no-recall gate in front of the ranker raises correct abstention on unanswerable prompts by at least 20 points while keeping gold retention within 0.02 of the ungated ranker; (3) opt-out compliance is measured separately, and the model gate earns its call on opt-out only if it beats a deterministic opt-out rule.
experiment.arms:
- Ranker factorial (none option x cutoff), same choice call, same pool, same order, same serving policy (serve up to 5 memory options that clear the cutoff, ranked by probability):
  - A00 (no none, no cutoff): top 5 memory options served; at least 1 always served (shipped Hindsight design).
  - A01 (no none, cutoff 0.05): memory options with probability >= 0.05, up to 5; empty if none clears.
  - B10 (none, no cutoff): top 5 memory options served, except serve nothing when the none option is the argmax.
  - B11 (none, cutoff 0.05): memory options with probability >= 0.05, up to 5; serve nothing when none is the argmax or no memory option clears (shipped jevmem design).
  - The none effect is estimated at each cutoff level (A00 vs B10, A01 vs B11); the cutoff effect is estimated separately (A00 vs A01). Losses from the cutoff are never attributed to the none option.
- Gate arms (ranker fixed at A00):
  - C: a yes/no model gate before retrieval ("Does answering this prompt need project memory? False if the prompt asks not to use memory."); on no, serve nothing; on yes, serve A00's result for that query (reused, not recomputed).
  - R: deterministic opt-out rule: a fixed, versioned phrase list ("without using memory", "don't use memory", "ignore project memory", and the variants in `optout_rules.txt`, frozen before prompts are written) serves nothing on a match; otherwise A00.
- Shared: pool = top 60 from H2's fusion (RRF k=60), candidate text truncated to 120 tokens, same seeded candidate order in every arm; ranker and gate use the same pinned decision model; the answerer and the judge are pinned models from different model families from each other and from the decision model; the judge sees only the prompt, the answer and the reference (or "unanswerable" label), never the arm, the served set or retrieval metadata. Order control: on a 100-query subset, A00 and B11 are re-run with two more seeded candidate orders.
experiment.metric: primary: (a) gold retention on answerable queries = |served intersect gold| / |gold|, 0 when nothing is served; (b) correct abstention on unanswerable prompts (the answerer declines or says unknown, per the blinded judge); (c) opt-out compliance on opt-out prompts (nothing served). Each is a separate endpoint; nothing is pooled. sections.question: Should "nothing relevant" be the reranker's call, or a separate check before we search at all?
sections.why_now:
**Two shipped systems made opposite choices without measuring abstention.**

We hold that a ranker must not be allowed to return nothing, and that "empty" belongs to a separate admission decision. We are about to specify the reranker on that basis. If we skip this, the reranker always serves at least one memory and a phrase list handles opt-outs.
sections.evidence:
**Weak: vendor numbers, unverified, pointing in opposite directions.**

One vendor reports that adding a "none of these" option emptied results on 35 of 200 questions, and dropped the share of right memories kept from 0.81 to 0.65. Another system ships the "none" option and states "recall quality is not measured". A third ships a check before retrieval with no accuracy numbers. The vendor articles were not available to the reviewer; the numbers only size the test.
sections.reviewer:
**Blocking until re-review; all three design findings addressed.**

The reviewer's findings on the earlier version:
- The "none" option and a probability cut-off were changed together, so losses could not be attributed. Now tested separately.
- Opt-out prompts inflated the check's score. Now scored separately against a fixed phrase list.
- The answering and judging models could be the same. Now separated and blinded.

Clears when: the reviewer accepts this version and the vendor articles are staged.

**Queues a six-person-day test on the shared retrieval harness.**

- Authorises: a queue place under caps of 30M tokens and 10 hours. Nothing runs until policy, runner and re-review exist.
- Cost: 6 people-days (3 writing and double-labelling prompts, 2 harness, 1 analysis). About $75 of model spend (25M tokens at our $3 per million planning rate).
- Shares candidate lists and the choice call with "Hosted listwise reranker versus a free local reranker"; building both together avoids duplicate harness work.
- Verdict: 2026-11-13, if the harness exists by 2026-10-30.
- Our pass bars: "none" costs at least 0.05 of right memories kept; the pre-check raises correct refusals on unanswerable prompts by at least 20 points while keeping memories within 0.02.
- Pass: empty answers come from the pre-check; the reranker never returns empty.
- Loss: the reranker may carry "none"; no pre-check model.
- Inconclusive: keep the shipped default; rerun at 250 unanswerable prompts.
sections.action:
**Approve: design is fixed; only re-review and harness remain.**

Approval queues it; the re-review must accept before anything runs.
sections.fits:
**Where recall decides to serve nothing.**

When an agent asks something, Engram retrieves candidate memories and a reranker picks the best few. Sometimes nothing is relevant, or the user says "without memory". This test decides which component says "serve nothing": the reranker itself, or a separate check that runs before retrieval. It refines the planned reranker and the rule for empty results in our first fixtures.

Revised spec E-20260926-04-r2 adds a non-curator cross-encoder rerank arm and pins pool depth, packing and the served-token ceiling. It requires Holm-adjusted intervals to ship curation or keep it as a rerank feature, separates an operational default from evidence of a small gain, and corrects the source reading (152 untouched test cases, not 503). It can move B7 (lead) against a strong-retrieval control before the H3 curate step ships; it stays queued while policy is unset.

experiment.claim: At a fixed served-token ceiling and identical candidate pool, task-conditioned curation at Spec time (H3) does not exceed anchored hybrid retrieval (top BM25 items first, then RRF fill) by 3 or more points of spec-task success; and a curator used as a reranker adds value only if it beats a non-curator cross-encoder reranker on the same candidates.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (strong-retrieval control): anchored hybrid: top-k BM25 hits first (k fixed on dev, default 5), then RRF (k=60) over vector, BM25 and entity channels, in that fused order.
- Arm B: H3 task-conditioned curation selecting from the same candidate pool.
- Arm C: Arm A's candidate pool reordered by the curator's scores.
- Arm D (added control): Arm A's candidate pool reordered by a non-curator cross-encoder reranker (bge-reranker-v2-m3, local, pinned). C is judged against D, so a gain from generic reranking is not credited to the curator.
- Shared across arms: candidate pool = top 50 from Arm A's retrieval (retrieval depth pinned); packing policy = whole items in each arm's rank order, skip an item that does not fit and continue, stop when the remaining budget is below the smallest remaining item; the served-token ceiling S is fixed on dev from {2,000, 4,000, 8,000} (default 4,000) and counted with the executor's tokenizer; actual served tokens are logged per task. Arms are matched on the served-token ceiling, not on total inference spend; curator and reranker cost is reported separately and any cost claim uses total spend.
- Same frozen executor and judge as H3. Executor, curator and judge are pinned to different models; the judge never sees arm labels or retrieval metadata.
experiment.metric: spec-task success as scored by the frozen H3 judge under H3's success rule (binary). Secondary: evidence recall on tasks with gold evidence; actual served tokens; total inference tokens and cost per task including curator or reranker; curator and reranker latency.
experiment.predeclared_margin: two primary comparisons, Holm-adjusted at family-wise 0.05: (1) B minus A; (2) C minus D. ship_B requires diff_BA >= 0.03 and the adjusted lower bound > 0. keep_C requires the adjusted lower bound of diff_CD > 0 and diff_CA >= 0.01. bound_B (evidence that curation's gain is below 3 points) requires the 95% upper bound of diff_BA < 0.03. Failing ship_B is not evidence of equivalence.
experiment.kill_criterion: diff_BA < 0 on the sealed test split (point estimate): curation is not shipped as a selector and survives only if keep_C holds. Stop before running (not a result) if the BM25 channel fails the preflight (P1: dead RediSearch prefix) or any pin is missing.

sections.question: Does a model that picks evidence for the task beat good plain search, at the same token budget?
sections.why_now:
**We are about to decide whether curation ships.**

Our belief that task-aware curation helps comes from a comparison against pre-written summaries, not against strong search. If we skip this, curation stays unshipped behind a flag and we keep paying for no decision.
sections.evidence:
**Moderate: one controlled study found planning lost to search.**

On 503 long-document multiple-choice questions, keyword-first hybrid search answered 36.18% correctly, a learned evidence planner 34.19%. On the 152 questions never used in training, 42.11% versus 36.84%, not statistically significant. Using the planner only to reorder results gained 1.79 points, also not significant. One benchmark, one 7B model, far from our spec tasks.
sections.reviewer:
**Blocking: firm verdicts are allowed on too little data.**

- The rules allow a "ship" or "no gain" verdict with only two test repositories.
- Curation must beat hybrid search but not the non-curator reranker, so it could ship while losing to a cheaper option.
- Token budget needs recomputing at the chosen evidence size.

Earlier findings (no plain reranker control, mismatched budgets, leakage across splits) were fixed.

Clears when: the reviewer accepts an 8-repository minimum and a comparison against the strongest non-curator option.
sections.commitment:
**Queues a five-person-day test likely to end in a default.**

- Authorises: a queue place under caps of 30M tokens and 24 hours. Nothing runs until policy, runner, search repair and fixes exist.
- Cost: 5 people-days (3.5 to extend the spec harness, 1.5 for analysis; the task set exists). About $66 of model spend (22M tokens at our $3 per million planning rate).
- Verdict: 2026-10-30, if the search repair and harness land by 2026-10-16.
- Power: with about 200 test tasks, only gains of 8 to 9 points are detectable, against our 3-point bar.
- Pass (curation at least 3 points better, interval above zero): curation ships.
- Loss (upper bound under 3 points): hybrid search is the selector.
- Inconclusive, the likely outcome: hybrid search becomes the default as the cheaper, deterministic option; curation stays flagged.
sections.action:
**Approve: it settles a shipping decision by 2026-10-30.**

A large curation win would show; otherwise we adopt the cheaper default with evidence rather than by assumption.
sections.fits:
**The step that picks evidence for an agent writing a spec.**

Before an agent writes a spec, Engram fills a fixed token budget with evidence. The planned design uses a model to curate that evidence for the task. This test compares it with strong plain search: keyword hits first, then a merged ranking of several search channels. It refines the planned spec-time curation work.

queue.proposed_experiment: Arm A = raw decision-model probabilities with fixed thresholds (content 0.5, injection 0.5); Arm B = isotonic recalibration fitted per source (chat turns, repo docs, tool output) on half the labels and scored on the other half, swapped and repeated 20 times; thresholds then chosen for 80% coverage. Dataset: at least 150 labelled save/skip turns and 150 labelled injection-gate lines per source (B21 sizes), labelled by someone other than the gate author. Metric: per-source ECE, calibration slope, precision at 80% coverage. Predeclared margin: ECE ratio A/B >= 2 on at least 2 of 3 sources and precision +3 points. It can move B14 (working) only by what the data show, before H5 and H10b set probability thresholds and bands; completing the packet is a prerequisite and it stays queued while policy is unset.

experiment.claim: For the save/skip write-admission gate and the served-memory injection gate, isotonic recalibration fitted per source (chat turns, repo docs, tool output) with cross-fitting over whole sessions or documents lowers the held-out Brier score relative to raw probabilities, with the cluster-bootstrap interval excluding zero, and lowers held-out ECE by at least 2x, on at least 2 of 3 sources for each gate. Selection precision at matched coverage is reported as a check, not claimed: within a source a monotone map preserves ranking, so it is expected not to change.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A: raw decision-model probabilities; for selection, the fixed production threshold 0.5 for both gates.
- Arm A2: raw probabilities with one threshold fitted on the fitting half, pooled across sources, targeting 80% coverage.
- Arm A3 (added control): raw probabilities with a threshold fitted per source on the fitting half at the same 80% coverage target and the same tie rule as Arm B. This separates source-specific thresholding from recalibration.
- Arm B: isotonic recalibration fitted per source on the fitting half; for selection, a per-source threshold at the same coverage target and tie rule.
- Arm B2 (secondary): Platt scaling with the same protocol.
- Coverage means, for the admission gate, the fraction of items saved; for the injection gate, the fraction of lines served (not blocked).
experiment.metric: calibration endpoint (primary): held-out Brier score and held-out log loss per source and gate (proper scoring rules), plus ECE with 10 equal-mass bins and calibration slope as corroboration. Selection endpoint (secondary, separate): precision at matched achieved coverage (each arm's threshold set at the scoring half's own 80% quantile, which isolates ranking) and precision at transferred threshold (fitting-half threshold applied to the scoring half, reporting the achieved coverage per arm). Gate-level precision is the unweighted mean over the three sources.
experiment.predeclared_margin: pass on a gate if, on at least 2 of 3 sources, Brier(A) - Brier(B) > 0 with the 95% cluster-bootstrap interval excluding 0 AND ECE(A) / max(ECE(B), 0.005) >= 2. Pass overall requires both gates to pass. Selection check: B minus A3 precision at matched achieved coverage is expected within +/-1 point; a larger difference is reported as a tie-handling or threshold-transfer effect and is not credited to recalibration.
experiment.kill_criterion: for both gates, on all three sources, the 95% interval of Brier(A) - Brier(B) includes 0 and ECE ratio < 1.3. Stop before running (not a result) if any source and gate has fewer than 150 items, fewer than 20 positives or 20 negatives, or items without a cluster id.

sections.question: Does a 70% score from our gates really mean 70%, and does correcting it per source help?
sections.why_now:
**We are about to set thresholds and escalation bands on these numbers.**

The escalation design sends cases scoring 0.3 to 0.7 to a stronger model, which assumes the scores are honest. The default if we skip this: fixed 0.5 cut-offs on raw vendor scores, the same for every source.
sections.evidence:
**Moderate: one paper, one benchmark, clean method.**

On crash-report classification, adjusting raw model scores cut average calibration error from 0.0231 to 0.0069, a 3.3x improvement, with training and testing on separate reports. Per-variable error ranged from 0.012 to 0.046. The paper notes that such adjustment keeps the ranking, so it improves the meaning of a score, not which items get picked. Two other figures on the original card were never fetched and are not used.
sections.reviewer:
**Blocking: statistical details, not the core question.**

- The error measure differs from the paper's, so the power estimate borrows numbers that do not compare.
- Nothing forces enough independent sessions per fit; all positives could sit in one session.
- The kill rule lumps "recalibration made it worse" with "no gain".

Earlier findings (source-specific thresholds confused with recalibration, sessions split across halves) were fixed.

Clears when: the reviewer accepts these three fixes.

sections.fits:
**Two filters: one decides what to save, one what to show.**

The save filter decides whether a new item enters memory. The show filter checks a memory line before an agent sees it. Both output a probability and cut at 0.5. This test asks whether that probability should be adjusted per source (chat, repo docs, tool output) first. It refines the planned escalation design and the planned filter evaluation.

queue.claim: On our labelled escalation set, the input-feature escalation classifier's leave-one-repository-out AUC is at least 0.10 below its item-level AUC and within 0.03 of a per-repository base-rate oracle, while an output-feature deferral rule keeps at least 0.05 more AUC under leave-one-repository-out.
queue.proposed_experiment: Arm A = input-feature escalation classifier (current H5 design) evaluated item-level 5-fold; Arm A' = same classifier evaluated leave-one-repository-out and with labels shuffled within repository; Arm B = deferral rule on the tier-1 output (answer length, abstain markers, confidence spread) evaluated leave-one-repository-out. Dataset: the H5 labelled turns grouped by repository (at least 6 repositories, 300 turns). Metric: AUC for "tier 2 changes the decision", plus shuffle-retention ratio. Predeclared margin: if Arm A' shuffle retains >= 85% of Arm A AUC, the classifier is declared group-memorising. Kill: if leave-one-repository-out AUC of Arm A is within 0.03 of item-level, drop this card (no group effect).
queue.why_it_matters: R6 requires that an evaluation support its conclusion; a gate that only recognises which repository a turn came from will fail on the next repository. The result decides how every R4 gate in the stack is evaluated before it ships.
queue.decision_it_could_change: whether the H5 escalation classifier is judged on item-level splits or on leave-one-repository-out plus shuffle controls, and whether escalation keys on input features or on the cheap tier's output

decision_chain.reason: Can move B13 (lead) with our own measurement: a repo-pinned note with within-group shuffle and leave-one-group-out controls shows item-level AUC collapsing to the group oracle, and H5 does not include those controls or an output-feature deferral arm. Revised spec E-20260926-02-r2 replaces the raw shuffle-retention verdict with a within-repository permutation test that only corroborates a repository-held-out gap. It also uses within-repository AUC with separate group-rate and constant baselines, symmetric equivalence, ordered verdicts, a pre-registered power simulation and a capped 300-call backfill. It can move B13 (lead) with our own group-held-out measurement before H5's escalation verdict, and output-feature escalation now depends only on its own comparison; it stays queued while policy is unset.

experiment.claim: On our labelled escalation set, the input-feature escalation classifier's within-repository AUC under leave-one-repository-out (LORO) evaluation is at least 0.10 below its within-repository AUC under session-grouped cross-validation, and its session-grouped signal does not exceed a within-repository label-permutation null (permutation p >= 0.05); separately, a deferral model on tier-1 output features has at least 0.05 higher LORO within-repository AUC than the input-feature classifier, with the repository-clustered interval excluding zero.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (session-grouped CV): the H5 input-feature escalation classifier, 5-fold cross-validation with folds grouped by session (turns of one session never straddle folds) and stratified by label. The only difference from Arm A-LORO is whether repositories are shared between train and test.
- Arm A-LORO: same classifier, features and hyperparameters, trained on all repositories but one and scored on the held-out repository, for each qualifying repository.
- Arm A-perm (permutation null): Arm A's session-grouped protocol with training-fold labels permuted within repository (each repository's base rate preserved), 200 permutations; every evaluation uses the untouched true test labels.
- Baseline G-item (group-rate, session-grouped): predicts each test item's repository training-fold escalation rate. Its pooled AUC measures how much AUC repository identity alone buys when repositories are shared across folds.
- Baseline G-LORO (constant): under LORO, the pooled training rate, constant within the held-out repository; its within-repository AUC is 0.5 by construction and it is reported only to make that explicit.
- Arm B: deferral model on tier-1 output features (answer length in tokens, abstain or hedge markers, confidence spread across tier-1 components), logistic regression, scored LORO.
experiment.metric: primary statistic for every arm: within-repository AUC = mean over qualifying repositories of the per-repository AUC, weighted by (positives x negatives) in that repository. Pooled out-of-fold AUC is reported but never decides, because pooling mixes fold priors. Label: 1 if the tier-2 decision differs from tier 1 and matches the gold label. Secondary: permutation p-value; pooled AUC of G-item; label test-retest kappa on a 50-item blind relabel.
experiment.predeclared_margin: group_memorisation requires ALL of: (auc_A - auc_A_loro) >= 0.10 with the repository-clustered 95% interval excluding 0; permutation p for Arm A >= 0.05 (no within-repository signal beyond base rate); auc_A >= 0.60 (the classifier has signal to lose). no_group_effect requires the 90% repository-clustered interval of (auc_A - auc_A_loro) to lie inside [-0.03, +0.03] (two one-sided tests; symmetric equivalence). prefer_output requires (auc_B - auc_A_loro) >= 0.05 with the 95% interval excluding 0. prefer_output is evaluated independently and is the only result that can change what escalation keys on.
experiment.kill_criterion: the no_group_effect verdict (equivalence within +/-0.03) ends the card with a negative result. Stop before running (not a result) if the preflight fails: fewer than 300 turns, fewer than 6 qualifying repositories, fewer than 60 positives overall, any feature derived from tier-2 output or gold, or more than 300 items missing tier-1 output.
